card.profile_long:
Nagila is a recreational solo dance tradition practiced by the Kassena and Frafra people residing in the Upper East region of Ghana. Primarily performed during community festivals and festive gatherings for entertainment, the dance serves as a vibrant focal point of social celebration. The physical execution of Nagila is distinct and demanding, characterized by a solo performer occupying the center of the performance space while engaging in a direct, dynamic interaction with the percussion ensemble. 

When a participant takes the center stage, they immediately establish the characteristic posture of the genre. The dancer bends their upper body forward to the extent that their hips and thighs form a precise right angle. In this lowered, forward-leaning stance, the arms are positioned with elbows held either in front or behind the torso. From this posture, the dancer stamps their feet on the ground in a continuous, rhythmic pattern that matches the pulse of the drums. 

Performance structure follows a strict cyclical pattern governed by duration and auditory cues. A single turn typically consists of the dancer moving vigorously for thirty seconds. Following this burst, the dancer pauses while the musical instruments continue to play alone for an interval. To signal that the dancer is ready to resume their physical movement, the drums increase in volume. This alternation between thirty-second dancing phases and musical interludes is repeated approximately six times before the current performer yields the center to a new dancer.

Musically, the performance is driven by drums that dictate both the rhythm of the foot-stamping and the structural transitions of the performance. The dynamic shifts—specifically the crescendo of the drums—act as an unstated command for the dancer to re-engage. While detailed descriptions of costumes, specific temporal meters, and historical timelines beyond regional association remain undocumented in current sources, the living tradition continues to thrive as an expression of community identity and rhythmic mastery among the Kassena and Frafra peoples.
